items.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010
items.q: he had a lot of originals that sounded like between Monk and Duke and Horace

ctx.x: Sadik Hakim. Yeah. He’s dead. But he lived in the lower East side and, but he was a real jazzer man. He kind of played between, he had originals, he wrote thousands of tunes and he had a lot of originals that sounded like between Monk and Duke and Horace, you know those kinds of tunes. He wrote great tunes. And every time — he was pretty famous so he would do a lot of trio gigs. And he would have quartet gigs and he would use me, because I would go play with him a lot and I liked his tunes, so we got along, I…

didn’t bother me because of the way I grew up. That’s why I didn’t mean to tell you this long story but you asked the question and I had a history with it. I never thought that way because I know it’s black music, that’s why I like it. You know, because to me this music is killing. I really don’t like white music, to tell you the truth. I’m serious. That’s what bothers me sometimes about rock & roll too, it’s just a little too Caucasian for me, and I’m just telling you the truth okay. That’s the way I grew up,…
